topic: Why does your stomach not digest itself?
q1_text: What is the main phenomenon studied when we ask why the stomach does not digest itself?
q1_a: The stomach produces no acid when it is not digesting food.
q1_b: Stomach cells are made of a special acid-proof protein called keratase.
q1_c: The stomach lining is protected by a thick layer of mucus that neutralises acid.
q2_text: Why is understanding the cause-and-effect mechanism more useful than just memorising the answer?
q2_a: Memorised answers are always correct, so mechanisms are unnecessary.
q2_b: Mechanisms only apply to chemistry, not to biology or physics.
q2_c: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q3_text: If the mucus lining of the stomach were damaged, what would you predict would happen?
q3_a: The stomach would produce less hydrochloric acid to compensate for the damage.
q3_b: Digestion would slow down because enzymes would have less space to work.
q3_c: Stomach acid could begin to digest the stomach wall, causing ulcers.

topic: How does the human nose actually work?
q1_text: What is the primary role of the olfactory receptors in the nose?
q1_a: Olfactory receptor cells detect chemical molecules in the air and send signals to the brain.
q1_b: Olfactory receptors filter dust particles before air enters the lungs.
q1_c: Olfactory receptors warm and humidify incoming air to protect the throat.
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism of smell more useful than just knowing that the nose detects odours?
q2_a: Knowing odours exist is enough; the mechanism adds no practical value.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: The mechanism of smell is too complex to be studied at Class 7 level.
q3_text: If the olfactory nerve were blocked, what would you predict would happen to a person's sense of smell?
q3_a: The person would lose the sense of smell because signals could not reach the brain.
q3_b: The person would smell more strongly because signals would build up in the receptors.
q3_c: The nose would produce more mucus to compensate for the missing nerve signals.

topic: Why do we breathe faster after running?
q1_text: What is the main reason we breathe faster after running?
q1_a: Muscles use more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide during exercise, so breathing rate increases to meet demand.
q1_b: Running heats the lungs, which makes the diaphragm contract more rapidly automatically.
q1_c: The body needs to cool down quickly, so it exhales hot air faster.
q2_text: Why is knowing the mechanism of increased breathing rate more useful than memorising that we breathe faster?
q2_a: The mechanism is only useful for doctors, not for students.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Memorising the fact is sufficient because breathing rate never changes.
q3_text: If a person held their breath after sprinting, what would you predict would happen?
q3_a: The muscles would stop producing carbon dioxide to prevent overload.
q3_b: Carbon dioxide levels in the blood would rise rapidly, triggering an urgent urge to breathe.
q3_c: The heart would slow down to reduce the demand for oxygen.

topic: How does blood know where to go?
q1_text: What guides blood to the correct organs in the circulatory system?
q1_a: Blood is pumped by the heart through a network of arteries, veins, and capillaries that form closed pathways to each organ.
q1_b: Blood cells have small magnets that attract them to specific organs needing oxygen.
q1_c: The brain sends electrical signals directly to red blood cells to direct their movement.
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism of blood circulation more useful than simply knowing blood travels around the body?
q2_a: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_b: Blood circulation is the same in all animals, so the mechanism never changes.
q2_c: The heart pumps randomly, so there is no predictable mechanism to study.
q3_text: If a major artery supplying a muscle were blocked, what would you predict would happen?
q3_a: The muscle would receive more blood from veins to compensate for the blocked artery.
q3_b: The heart would beat slower to reduce pressure in the blocked vessel.
q3_c: The muscle would be deprived of oxygen and begin to fail or cramp.

topic: Why do plants need sunlight?
q1_text: What is the main reason plants need sunlight?
q1_a: Sunlight provides energy for photosynthesis, the process by which plants make food from carbon dioxide and water.
q1_b: Sunlight heats the roots, which allows water to be absorbed more efficiently from the soil.
q1_c: Plants use sunlight to produce oxygen directly from the soil without needing carbon dioxide.
q2_text: Why is understanding the mechanism of photosynthesis more useful than knowing that plants need sunlight?
q2_a: Plants grow identically in all light conditions, so the mechanism does not matter.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Only botanists need to understand photosynthesis; other students can memorise the fact.
q3_text: If a plant were kept in complete darkness for several weeks, what would you predict would happen?
q3_a: The plant would be unable to make food, weaken, and eventually die.
q3_b: The plant would switch to absorbing nitrogen from the air to replace lost glucose.
q3_c: The plant would grow faster because darkness accelerates cell division in stems.

topic: How does a seed know which way to grow?
q1_text: What is the main mechanism that tells a seed's root to grow downward and shoot to grow upward?
q1_a: A process called gravitropism makes roots grow toward gravity and shoots grow away from it.
q1_b: Seeds detect the colour of soil and grow their roots toward darker regions.
q1_c: The seed's outer coat has markings that orient the embryo correctly before germination.
q2_text: Why is knowing the mechanism of directional growth more useful than just observing that roots grow down?
q2_a: Roots always grow in random directions, so there is no mechanism to study.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Seed growth direction is determined only by the farmer planting the seed correctly.
q3_text: If a germinating seed were grown in a rotating drum that cancelled out the effect of gravity, what would you predict?
q3_a: The root would grow faster because less gravity means less resistance to elongation.
q3_b: The shoot would grow downward because photosynthesis requires the leaves to face the soil.
q3_c: The root and shoot would grow in random directions, unable to use gravity as a guide.

topic: Why do some materials float while others sink?
q1_text: What determines whether an object floats or sinks in water?
q1_a: An object floats if it is made of natural materials and sinks if it is made of synthetic ones.
q1_b: An object floats if its density is less than water and sinks if its density is greater than water.
q1_c: An object floats only if it is hollow and sinks only if it is completely solid.
q2_text: Why is understanding density and buoyancy more useful than just knowing which objects float?
q2_a: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_b: Every object floats in water, so there is no need to understand the mechanism.
q2_c: Buoyancy only applies to water, so the mechanism has no real-world applications.
q3_text: If you added salt to water until it became very dense, what would you predict would happen to an egg placed in it?
q3_a: The egg would float because the saltwater's density becomes greater than the egg's density.
q3_b: The egg would sink faster because salt increases the gravitational pull on objects.
q3_c: The egg would dissolve because salt reacts chemically with the eggshell.

topic: The hidden world inside a drop of water
q1_text: What is found in a drop of pond water that cannot be seen with the naked eye?
q1_a: A drop of water contains tiny air pockets that give it its round shape on surfaces.
q1_b: Water droplets contain dissolved minerals arranged in crystal patterns invisible to the eye.
q1_c: Microscopic living organisms such as bacteria, algae, and protozoa exist in a drop of pond water.
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism of what makes water life-supporting more useful than just knowing microbes exist?
q2_a: All microbes are harmful, so understanding them has no benefit for students.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Microbes in water are destroyed by oxygen, so the mechanism is always the same.
q3_text: If the water in a pond were heated to a very high temperature, what would you predict would happen to the microorganisms?
q3_a: The microorganisms would grow larger because heat provides them with more energy.
q3_b: Most microorganisms would be killed by the heat, drastically reducing their population.
q3_c: The microorganisms would move to the bottom of the pond to avoid the heat.

topic: Why does ice float on water?
q1_text: What is the main reason ice floats on liquid water?
q1_a: Ice floats because it contains trapped air bubbles that make it lighter than water.
q1_b: Ice is less dense than liquid water because water molecules form a hexagonal crystal structure when frozen, taking up more space.
q1_c: Ice floats because its surface is smoother, reducing the friction that would make it sink.
q2_text: Why is understanding the molecular structure of ice more useful than knowing that ice floats?
q2_a: Ice always sinks in warm water, so the molecular explanation is incorrect.
q2_b: The floating of ice is only important in polar regions and not relevant elsewhere.
q2_c: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q3_text: What would happen to aquatic life in lakes if ice were denser than water and sank to the bottom?
q3_a: Fish would swim to the surface in winter because warm water rises to replace sinking ice.
q3_b: Lakes would freeze more slowly because sunlight would not be blocked by a floating ice layer.
q3_c: Lakes would freeze solid from the bottom up, killing most aquatic life in winter.

topic: How does a refrigerator actually cool things?
q1_text: What is the basic mechanism by which a refrigerator cools food?
q1_a: A refrigerant fluid circulates through coils, evaporating inside the fridge to absorb heat and condensing outside to release it.
q1_b: The refrigerator generates cold air by spinning a fan through ice water stored in the back panel.
q1_c: Electric current flowing through metal coils directly absorbs heat from the food inside.
q2_text: Why is understanding the refrigeration cycle more useful than knowing that a refrigerator keeps things cold?
q2_a: Refrigerators produce cold from nothing, so there is no mechanism to explain.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: All appliances work the same way, so understanding one mechanism explains nothing new.
q3_text: If the refrigerant fluid in a refrigerator leaked out completely, what would you predict would happen?
q3_a: The fridge would cool more efficiently because air conducts cold better than refrigerant.
q3_b: The compressor would produce more electrical energy to compensate for the missing refrigerant.
q3_c: The refrigerator would stop cooling because there is no fluid to carry heat away from inside.

topic: Why do shadows change during the day?
q1_text: What is the main reason shadows change length and direction during the day?
q1_a: The Moon's gravitational pull bends sunlight differently at different times of the day.
q1_b: As the Earth rotates, the Sun's apparent position in the sky changes, altering the angle of light and therefore the shadow's length and direction.
q1_c: Shadows change because the temperature of the air bends light rays by different amounts.
q2_text: Why is understanding Earth's rotation more useful than just observing that shadows move?
q2_a: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_b: Shadows are caused by clouds, so Earth's rotation plays no role in their movement.
q2_c: Shadow movement is random and cannot be predicted by any mechanism.
q3_text: If you measured the length of your shadow at noon and again at 4 PM, what would you predict?
q3_a: The shadow would be longer at noon because the Sun is directly overhead and very hot.
q3_b: The shadow would be longer at 4 PM because the Sun is lower in the sky at that time.
q3_c: The shadow would be the same length because the Sun moves at a constant speed.

topic: How does a mirror produce your image?
q1_text: What is the mechanism by which a flat mirror produces a reflection of your face?
q1_a: Light rays from your face hit the smooth mirror surface and bounce back at equal but opposite angles, forming a virtual image.
q1_b: Mirrors contain a thin film of glass that stores a photographic imprint of whatever is in front of it.
q1_c: The silver coating in a mirror emits its own light shaped like the object placed in front of it.
q2_text: Why is understanding how light reflects off mirrors more useful than knowing mirrors show your image?
q2_a: All surfaces reflect light equally, so the mechanism of mirrors is not unique.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Mirror reflections are an optical illusion and cannot be explained by a mechanism.
q3_text: If you covered a mirror with a rough, uneven coating, what would you predict would happen to the reflection?
q3_a: The image would become sharper because rough surfaces scatter light more precisely.
q3_b: The image would become blurry or disappear because the rough surface scatters light in many directions.
q3_c: The image would become brighter because roughness increases the amount of light reflected.

topic: Why does sound disappear in space?
q1_text: What is the main reason sound cannot travel through space?
q1_a: Sound disappears in space because the cold temperature freezes the sound waves instantly.
q1_b: Gravity in space is too weak to carry sound vibrations between objects.
q1_c: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs a medium of particles to travel through; space is a vacuum with no particles.
q2_text: Why is understanding that sound needs a medium more useful than just knowing sound cannot travel in space?
q2_a: Sound actually travels faster in space than on Earth, so the medium does not matter.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Space is full of invisible gas, so the explanation about a vacuum is incorrect.
q3_text: If astronauts in space suits needed to communicate, what would you predict would work and what would not?
q3_a: Shouting loudly would work because space suits amplify sound vibrations significantly.
q3_b: Tapping helmets together would be enough because vibrations travel well through any vacuum.
q3_c: Radio waves would work but direct voice communication through the vacuum would fail.

topic: How does your ear turn sound into signals?
q1_text: What is the mechanism by which the ear converts sound waves into nerve signals?
q1_a: Sound waves make the eardrum vibrate; tiny bones amplify this vibration and the cochlea converts it to electrical nerve signals.
q1_b: Sound waves are absorbed by the ear canal lining, which contains chemical sensors that detect pitch.
q1_c: The ear funnels sound into the brain directly through the auditory canal without any vibrating structures.
q2_text: Why is understanding the mechanism of hearing more useful than knowing that ears detect sound?
q2_a: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_b: The ear is too complex to have a mechanism; it works like a magic receiver.
q2_c: All animals hear identically, so understanding the human ear explains nothing new.
q3_text: If the tiny bones (ossicles) inside a person's ear were damaged, what would you predict would happen?
q3_a: The person would hear more clearly because fewer parts would interfere with sound transmission.
q3_b: Hearing would be significantly reduced because vibrations could not be amplified and sent to the cochlea.
q3_c: The eardrum would vibrate more strongly to compensate for the missing bone movement.

topic: Why does a bicycle stay upright?
q1_text: What is the main mechanism that keeps a moving bicycle balanced upright?
q1_a: Bicycles stay upright because the weight of the rider presses evenly on both sides of the frame.
q1_b: A moving bicycle stays upright through gyroscopic effects of spinning wheels and the rider making small steering corrections.
q1_c: The rubber tyres create a magnetic interaction with the road that prevents the bicycle from falling.
q2_text: Why is understanding the physics of bicycle balance more useful than knowing a bicycle stays upright?
q2_a: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_b: Bicycles always fall over when stationary, so the mechanism only works when moving.
q2_c: Balance is a skill only humans have, so the mechanism cannot be described scientifically.
q3_text: If a bicycle were moving very slowly, what would you predict about its stability compared to a fast-moving bicycle?
q3_a: A slow bicycle would be more stable because lower speed reduces vibrations in the wheels.
q3_b: Speed has no effect on bicycle stability because the frame provides all the balance.
q3_c: A slow bicycle would be less stable because the gyroscopic effect of spinning wheels is weaker at low speed.

topic: What makes electricity flow?
q1_text: What causes electric current to flow through a conductor?
q1_a: Electricity flows because atoms in a wire vibrate and bump into each other, passing energy along.
q1_b: Current flows because positive charges in the wire are attracted toward the negative terminal of a battery.
q1_c: A potential difference (voltage) pushes free electrons through a conductor, creating an electric current.
q2_text: Why is understanding voltage and electron flow more useful than knowing that electricity comes from a battery?
q2_a: Batteries produce magic energy that cannot be explained by electron movement.
q2_b: Electrons never actually move in a wire; only energy moves, so the mechanism is irrelevant.
q2_c: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q3_text: If you connected a wire between the two terminals of a battery without any bulb or resistor, what would you predict?
q3_a: A very large current would flow, heating the wire rapidly and quickly draining the battery.
q3_b: No current would flow because a bulb is required to complete the circuit.
q3_c: The battery would produce light instead of current because the circuit is incomplete.

topic: Why does a compass point north?
q1_text: What is the main reason a compass needle always points toward magnetic north?
q1_a: The North Star exerts a gravitational pull on the iron in compass needles pointing them northward.
q1_b: The Earth behaves like a giant magnet, and the compass needle aligns with Earth's magnetic field lines.
q1_c: Compass needles are electrically charged and are attracted to the cold air found at the North Pole.
q2_text: Why is understanding Earth's magnetic field more useful than simply knowing a compass points north?
q2_a: A compass always points to true geographic north, so the magnetic field plays no role.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Magnetic fields are invisible and cannot be detected, so they are not useful to study.
q3_text: If you placed a compass near a strong iron bar magnet, what would you predict would happen?
q3_a: The compass would stop working because the iron would absorb all magnetic fields nearby.
q3_b: The compass needle would be deflected from north and point toward the bar magnet's poles instead.
q3_c: The compass needle would point toward geographic north even more accurately near the magnet.

topic: How do magnets work without touching?
q1_text: What is the mechanism that allows magnets to attract or repel objects without physical contact?
q1_a: Magnets release tiny invisible particles called magnetons that physically push or pull on other objects.
q1_b: Magnets attract objects by generating a static electric charge on their surface that grips metal.
q1_c: Magnets create an invisible magnetic field in the surrounding space; objects within this field experience a force.
q2_text: Why is understanding magnetic fields more useful than knowing that magnets attract iron?
q2_a: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_b: Magnets only attract iron, so the field concept is unnecessary for other materials.
q2_c: Magnetic forces only work when magnets are in direct contact, so fields are not real.
q3_text: If you increased the distance between two attracting magnets, what would you predict would happen to the force between them?
q3_a: The force would stay the same because magnetic fields are uniform throughout space.
q3_b: The force would decrease because the magnetic field becomes weaker with increasing distance.
q3_c: The force would increase because the magnetic field spreads out and becomes stronger farther away.

topic: Why does iron rust?
q1_text: What is the chemical process that causes iron to rust?
q1_a: Iron absorbs carbon dioxide from the air, which breaks down its surface into a reddish powder.
q1_b: Iron rusts because the heat from sunlight causes the metal atoms to break apart and turn red.
q1_c: Iron reacts with oxygen and water in the environment to form iron oxide, commonly known as rust.
q2_text: Why is understanding the chemistry of rusting more useful than knowing that iron turns reddish-brown?
q2_a: Rust is only a colour change and does not involve any chemical reaction.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Rusting happens only in coastal areas, so the mechanism is not generally applicable.
q3_text: If you coated an iron nail with a layer of paint before leaving it outside, what would you predict?
q3_a: The nail would rust much more slowly because paint prevents oxygen and water from reaching the iron.
q3_b: The nail would rust faster because paint traps moisture against the iron surface.
q3_c: The nail would rust from the inside outward because paint blocks oxygen from escaping.

topic: What happens when food is digested?
q1_text: What is the main process that happens when food is digested in the body?
q1_a: Food is burned by stomach heat to release energy directly into the muscles.
q1_b: Large food molecules are broken down by enzymes and acids into small nutrients that can be absorbed into the blood.
q1_c: Food is compressed by the stomach into a liquid form that the body uses as fuel without chemical change.
q2_text: Why is understanding the enzyme-driven mechanism of digestion more useful than knowing food gets broken down?
q2_a: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_b: Food is digested by heat alone, so enzymes play no role in the process.
q2_c: Digestion is identical in all animals, so studying the mechanism adds no new knowledge.
q3_text: If a person's body could not produce the enzyme amylase, what would you predict about their digestion of starch?
q3_a: Starch would be digested faster because the body would use acids instead of enzymes.
q3_b: Starch would not be broken down into sugars, causing poor absorption of carbohydrate energy.
q3_c: The person would absorb more starch directly through the stomach wall without breaking it down.

topic: How do vaccines teach the immune system?
q1_text: What is the mechanism by which vaccines protect a person against disease?
q1_a: Vaccines inject chemical antibiotics that remain in the blood and kill any invading bacteria or viruses.
q1_b: A vaccine introduces a harmless form of a pathogen, training the immune system to produce antibodies before real infection occurs.
q1_c: Vaccines strengthen the skin barrier to prevent viruses from entering the body through cuts.
q2_text: Why is understanding how the immune system is trained by vaccines more useful than knowing vaccines prevent disease?
q2_a: Vaccines work instantly and permanently, so the training mechanism does not matter.
q2_b: The immune system destroys all vaccines before they can have any effect on the body.
q2_c: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q3_text: If a vaccine only produced a very weak immune response, what would you predict about protection against the real disease?
q3_a: The person would have inadequate protection because too few antibodies would be available to fight the real infection.
q3_b: The person would be fully protected because even a small number of antibodies is enough.
q3_c: The person would become immune faster because a weak response is less tiring for the body.

topic: Why do we get fever?
q1_text: What is the main biological reason the body produces a fever when infected?
q1_a: Fever is caused by the body burning extra calories to produce antibodies, releasing heat as a by-product.
q1_b: White blood cells generate fever to signal the brain to stop all normal body functions temporarily.
q1_c: The immune system raises body temperature to slow the growth of pathogens and speed up immune cell activity.
q2_text: Why is understanding the purpose of fever more useful than knowing that body temperature rises during illness?
q2_a: Fever is always harmful and has no useful purpose, so there is no beneficial mechanism.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Fever is caused only by environmental heat and has nothing to do with the immune system.
q3_text: If a patient's fever became dangerously high (above 41°C), what would you predict about the risk to the body?
q3_a: An extremely high fever would kill all pathogens instantly, curing the infection permanently.
q3_b: An extremely high fever could damage brain cells and other tissues because proteins start to denature above safe temperatures.
q3_c: A very high fever would boost the immune response so strongly that the body heals in hours.

topic: How do forests create rain?
q1_text: What is the main mechanism by which forests contribute to rainfall?
q1_a: Trees release water vapour through transpiration; this vapour rises, cools, and condenses to form clouds that produce rain.
q1_b: Forest soil absorbs rainwater and then shoots it upward as water vapour through tiny root pores.
q1_c: Trees attract rain clouds magnetically because their tall canopies create an electrical charge in the atmosphere.
q2_text: Why is understanding the transpiration-precipitation cycle more useful than knowing forests produce rain?
q2_a: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_b: Rain is produced only by the ocean; forests have no effect on rainfall at all.
q2_c: All vegetation produces identical amounts of water vapour, so forests are not special.
q3_text: If a large forest were completely cut down, what would you predict would happen to the local rainfall over time?
q3_a: Rainfall would increase because bare land absorbs more solar energy and heats the air more.
q3_b: Rainfall would remain unchanged because clouds form independently of the vegetation below them.
q3_c: Rainfall would decrease because less transpiration means less water vapour available to form clouds.

topic: Why is the sky blue?
q1_text: What is the main reason the sky appears blue during the day?
q1_a: The sky reflects blue light from the oceans, which cover most of the Earth's surface.
q1_b: The atmosphere scatters blue light from sunlight more than other colours because blue has a shorter wavelength; this scattered blue light reaches our eyes from all directions.
q1_c: Blue gas molecules in the upper atmosphere absorb all other colours of sunlight and emit only blue light.
q2_text: Why is understanding Rayleigh scattering more useful than just knowing the sky looks blue?
q2_a: The sky is only blue in tropical countries; in other regions it is a different colour.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Light scattering is the same for all colours, so Rayleigh scattering explains nothing special.
q3_text: Why does the sky look red or orange during sunrise and sunset rather than blue?
q3_a: The Sun produces more red light in the morning and evening because it is cooler at those times.
q3_b: Sunlight travels through more atmosphere near the horizon, scattering away most blue light and leaving red and orange.
q3_c: Clouds reflect the orange colour of the ground, making the sky appear reddish near the horizon.

topic: How do clouds form?
q1_text: What is the mechanism by which clouds form in the atmosphere?
q1_a: Clouds form when wind carries water directly from the ocean surface into the upper atmosphere as droplets.
q1_b: Water vapour in the atmosphere becomes heavy enough to clump together into visible clouds without needing to cool down.
q1_c: Warm moist air rises, cools at higher altitudes, and water vapour condenses around tiny dust particles to form cloud droplets.
q2_text: Why is understanding condensation and cloud formation more useful than knowing that clouds are made of water?
q2_a: Clouds are made of ice crystals in all conditions, so condensation plays no role in cloud formation.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Cloud formation cannot be predicted because weather is entirely random.
q3_text: If there were no dust particles in the atmosphere at all, what would you predict about cloud formation?
q3_a: Cloud formation would be greatly reduced because water vapour needs particles as condensation nuclei to form droplets.
q3_b: Clouds would form faster because clean air allows water vapour to condense more easily.
q3_c: Clouds would be larger and darker because pure water droplets contain more energy.

topic: Why do earthquakes happen?
q1_text: What is the main cause of earthquakes?
q1_a: Earthquakes are caused by large underground explosions of volcanic gas trapped beneath the Earth's crust.
q1_b: Earthquakes occur when underground rivers erode rock cavities until the ground above collapses inward.
q1_c: Earthquakes occur when tectonic plates move and the stress built up along their boundaries is suddenly released as seismic energy.
q2_text: Why is understanding tectonic plate movement more useful than knowing that earthquakes shake the ground?
q2_a: Tectonic plates do not move; earthquakes are caused entirely by human mining activities.
q2_b: All earthquakes are small and identical, so a detailed mechanism adds no value.
q2_c: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q3_text: If two tectonic plates had been locked together without moving for a very long time, what would you predict when they finally shifted?
q3_a: A large earthquake would likely occur because enormous stress energy built up during the locked period would be released suddenly.
q3_b: The plates would slide smoothly and cause no earthquake because the long rest reduced friction.
q3_c: A small tremor would occur but no major earthquake because the plates had cooled down over time.

topic: How do volcanoes work?
q1_text: What is the main mechanism that causes a volcano to erupt?
q1_a: Volcanoes erupt when underground water reacts chemically with iron-rich rocks to produce explosive gas.
q1_b: Volcanic eruptions are caused by the Earth spinning, which flings hot material toward the surface near the equator.
q1_c: Molten rock (magma) from inside the Earth rises through cracks in the crust due to pressure, reaching the surface as lava during an eruption.
q2_text: Why is understanding magma pressure and plate tectonics more useful than knowing volcanoes release lava?
q2_a: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_b: Volcanic eruptions are random events that cannot be explained by pressure or plate movement.
q2_c: All volcanoes erupt identically, so understanding the mechanism explains no differences between them.
q3_text: If pressure inside a volcano continued to build without any eruption for a very long time, what would you predict?
q3_a: An extremely powerful eruption would eventually occur when the pressure exceeded the strength of the surrounding rock.
q3_b: The pressure would eventually stabilise on its own as the magma cooled and solidified underground.
q3_c: The volcano would become extinct because old pressure dissipates without erupting.

topic: Could humans live on Mars?
q1_text: What is the main challenge that makes it difficult for humans to live on Mars without special equipment?
q1_a: Mars has too much gravity for human bones and muscles to function normally without collapsing.
q1_b: Mars has a very thin atmosphere with almost no oxygen, extreme cold temperatures, and high radiation levels that are lethal without protection.
q1_c: Mars is covered entirely by liquid water oceans, making it impossible to build stable structures on the surface.
q2_text: Why is understanding the conditions on Mars more useful than simply knowing humans cannot currently live there?
q2_a: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_b: Mars is identical to Earth in all conditions, so there are no challenges to understand.
q2_c: Human space travel to Mars is impossible and will never happen, so studying conditions there is pointless.
q3_text: If scientists successfully created a pressurised habitat with breathable air on Mars, what remaining challenge would colonists still face?
q3_a: The colonists would face no further challenges because breathable air solves all survival problems on Mars.
q3_b: Colonists would need to deal with Mars's very strong magnetic field disrupting all electronic equipment.
q3_c: Colonists would still face extreme cold, harmful radiation, dust storms, and the need to grow food with limited resources.

topic: What would happen if Earth stopped rotating?
q1_text: What is the main effect Earth's rotation has on life and the environment?
q1_a: Earth's rotation creates gravity by spinning; without it objects would float off the surface into space.
q1_b: Earth's rotation powers photosynthesis in plants by ensuring every region receives equal amounts of sunlight each day.
q1_c: Earth's rotation creates the cycle of day and night, drives weather patterns through the Coriolis effect, and maintains the planet's oblate shape.
q2_text: Why is understanding the effects of Earth's rotation more useful than just knowing the Earth spins?
q2_a: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_b: Earth's rotation has no effect on weather, time, or life — it only affects satellite orbits.
q2_c: The Earth stopped rotating millions of years ago, so studying its current rotation is irrelevant.
q3_text: If Earth suddenly stopped rotating, what would you predict would happen to a person standing on the surface?
q3_a: The person would feel lighter because stopping rotation reduces centrifugal force on the equator.
q3_b: The person would experience no immediate change because gravity alone keeps people on the ground.
q3_c: The person would be thrown forward at tremendous speed due to inertia, as the surface stopped but the person kept moving.

topic: The Ultimate Challenge: Design a self-sustaining space habitat
q1_text: What is the central idea behind designing a self-sustaining space habitat?
q1_a: A self-sustaining habitat is one that is built from materials found in space without using any Earth-manufactured components.
q1_b: Self-sustainability in space means the habitat can operate for exactly one year before requiring a complete resupply mission.
q1_c: A self-sustaining habitat must recycle air, water, and waste while producing its own food and energy without resupply from Earth.
q2_text: Why is understanding the mechanism of closed-loop life support more useful than knowing a habitat needs air and food?
q2_a: Space habitats are supplied continuously from Earth, so closed-loop systems are unnecessary to study.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Oxygen in space can be captured directly from starlight, so understanding recycling is irrelevant.
q3_text: If the plant-growing system in a space habitat failed, what would you predict would happen to the crew over time?
q3_a: The crew would be unaffected because space habitats store enough packaged food for decades.
q3_b: The habitat's recycling system would automatically convert carbon dioxide back into food for the crew.
q3_c: The crew would face food shortages and rising carbon dioxide levels, as plants provide both food and oxygen recycling.

topic: What actually happens when you eat food?
q1_text: What is the correct sequence of digestion in the human body?
q1_a: Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine
q1_b: Mouth, stomach, oesophagus, large intestine, small intestine
q1_c: Oesophagus, mouth, stomach, small intestine, large intestine
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism of digestion more useful than memorising the result?
q2_a: Memorised facts are always accurate and never need updating
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction
q2_c: Results are easier to remember than mechanisms in biology
q3_text: If a person's stomach produced no acid, what would you predict?
q3_a: Food would be digested faster due to reduced friction
q3_b: More nutrients would be absorbed in the large intestine instead
q3_c: Protein digestion would be severely impaired

topic: The microscopic battle between bacteria and antibiotics
q1_text: How do antibiotics kill or stop bacteria?
q1_a: They target bacterial cell structures that human cells do not have
q1_b: They heat the bloodstream to kill bacteria through thermal shock
q1_c: They remove oxygen from tissues so bacteria cannot respire
q2_text: Why is understanding the mechanism of antibiotic resistance important?
q2_a: It helps doctors memorise drug names more easily
q2_b: Mechanisms are only useful for chemistry, not biology
q2_c: Knowing the mechanism helps predict and prevent resistance spreading
q3_text: If antibiotics are overused, what would you predict about bacteria?
q3_a: Bacteria would become larger and easier to detect under microscopes
q3_b: Bacteria would lose their ability to reproduce as quickly
q3_c: Resistant bacteria would survive and multiply, making treatment harder

topic: How does your immune system recognize an enemy?
q1_text: What does the immune system use to identify foreign invaders?
q1_a: The colour of pathogens is detected by white blood cells
q1_b: Body temperature rises and burns pathogens before recognition
q1_c: Antigens on the surface of pathogens trigger immune recognition
q2_text: Why is understanding the immune recognition mechanism useful?
q2_a: It allows doctors to memorise the names of all pathogens
q2_b: It explains how vaccines and immunity work, enabling predictions
q2_c: Immune mechanisms only apply to bacterial infections, not viruses
q3_text: If a person encountered a pathogen for the second time, what would you predict?
q3_a: The immune response would be faster due to memory B cells
q3_b: The immune response would be slower because antibodies degrade over time
q3_c: The body would have no memory of the pathogen and react identically

topic: Why does your heart beat continuously?
q1_text: What keeps the heart beating without conscious effort?
q1_a: Muscles in the chest wall compress the heart rhythmically
q1_b: The sinoatrial node generates electrical impulses that trigger contractions
q1_c: Blood pressure forces the heart valves to open and close repeatedly
q2_text: Why is knowing the mechanism of the heartbeat more useful than just knowing it beats?
q2_a: The heartbeat mechanism helps athletes run faster during exercise
q2_b: Knowing the mechanism allows us to understand heart disease and treatments
q2_c: Memorising the heartbeat rate is sufficient for all medical purposes
q3_text: If the sinoatrial node were damaged, what would you predict?
q3_a: The heart's rhythm would become irregular or stop
q3_b: The heart would beat faster to compensate for reduced signal strength
q3_c: Blood would circulate in the opposite direction through the veins

topic: How do neurons carry information?
q1_text: How do neurons transmit signals along their length?
q1_a: An electrical impulse called an action potential travels along the axon
q1_b: Neurons pass solid chemical pellets along hollow tubes to the brain
q1_c: Light signals travel through transparent neuron fibres to receptors
q2_text: Why is understanding the neural mechanism more useful than memorising nerve names?
q2_a: It enables predictions about what happens when nerves are damaged
q2_b: Nerve names are sufficient for understanding all neurological conditions
q2_c: Mechanisms only matter for motor neurons, not sensory neurons
q3_text: If the myelin sheath around a neuron were damaged, what would you predict?
q3_a: The neuron would generate stronger signals to overcome the damage
q3_b: The neuron would switch to chemical transmission instead of electrical
q3_c: Signal transmission would slow down or fail, causing nerve disorders

topic: Why do we have fingerprints?
q1_text: What is the primary function of fingerprint ridges on human skin?
q1_a: Fingerprints regulate sweat distribution to keep palms dry
q1_b: Fingerprint ridges improve grip by increasing friction between skin and objects
q1_c: Fingerprint patterns identify nerves under the skin for better sensation
q2_text: Why is understanding why fingerprints exist more useful than just describing their patterns?
q2_a: Pattern descriptions are sufficient for forensic science applications
q2_b: Fingerprint function only matters for primates, not humans specifically
q2_c: Understanding function allows predictions about people who lack fingerprints
q3_text: If fingerprint ridges were completely smooth, what would you predict?
q3_a: People would develop stronger nails to compensate for grip loss
q3_b: Sweat glands in the fingertip would become more active instead
q3_c: Grip on smooth or wet surfaces would be significantly reduced

topic: The science of friction
q1_text: What causes friction between two surfaces?
q1_a: Friction is caused by static electricity attracting surfaces together
q1_b: Microscopic irregularities on surfaces interlock and resist sliding motion
q1_c: Air molecules trapped between surfaces push back against movement
q2_text: Why is knowing how friction works more useful than just knowing it slows things down?
q2_a: Understanding friction helps engineers design brakes, tyres, and lubricants
q2_b: Knowing friction slows things down is enough for all engineering problems
q2_c: Friction mechanisms are only relevant to physics, not everyday engineering
q3_text: If a lubricant were applied between two sliding surfaces, what would you predict?
q3_a: Friction would decrease because the lubricant separates the surfaces
q3_b: Friction would increase because the lubricant adds extra mass to surfaces
q3_c: Surfaces would bond together as the lubricant hardens under pressure

topic: Why can a giant ship float?
q1_text: What principle explains why a massive steel ship can float on water?
q1_a: Steel becomes less dense when heated by the sun on open oceans
q1_b: Archimedes' principle: the ship displaces water equal to its weight
q1_c: Air currents beneath the hull push the ship upward like a wing
q2_text: Why does understanding buoyancy as a mechanism matter more than memorising that ships float?
q2_a: Memorising that ships float is sufficient for all naval engineering
q2_b: It lets engineers predict how much cargo a ship can safely carry
q2_c: Buoyancy mechanisms only apply to wooden boats, not steel ones
q3_text: If a ship took on water and became denser than water overall, what would you predict?
q3_a: The ship would sink because upthrust would no longer equal the total weight
q3_b: The ship would rise higher in the water due to increased internal pressure
q3_c: The ship's buoyancy force would increase to balance the extra weight

topic: How does pressure change with depth?
q1_text: What happens to water pressure as you go deeper underwater?
q1_a: Pressure decreases with depth because there is less air below the surface
q1_b: Pressure stays constant at any depth because water is incompressible
q1_c: Pressure increases with depth because the weight of water above increases
q2_text: Why is understanding the pressure-depth mechanism useful?
q2_a: Memorising that deep water is dangerous is sufficient for all purposes
q2_b: Pressure mechanisms only matter for gases, not liquids like water
q2_c: It helps predict safe diving depths and design submarines and pipelines
q3_text: If a submarine descended to twice the depth, what would you predict about external pressure?
q3_a: External pressure would remain the same because water density is constant
q3_b: Pressure would decrease as colder water is less able to exert force
q3_c: External pressure would approximately double due to greater water weight above

topic: Why does a balloon expand at high altitude?
q1_text: Why does a sealed balloon get bigger when it rises to high altitude?
q1_a: Atmospheric pressure decreases at altitude, allowing the gas inside to expand
q1_b: Warmer temperatures at altitude cause the rubber to stretch outward
q1_c: Gravity decreases at altitude so gas molecules spread apart naturally
q2_text: Why is knowing the mechanism of gas expansion more useful than just observing it expands?
q2_a: Observing the expansion is enough to design weather balloons accurately
q2_b: It enables predictions about balloon volume at different altitudes or pressures
q2_c: Gas expansion mechanisms only apply to helium, not to air-filled balloons
q3_text: If a balloon were taken deep underwater instead, what would you predict?
q3_a: The balloon would shrink because increased pressure compresses the gas inside
q3_b: The balloon would expand as water is denser and pushes gas outward
q3_c: The balloon would stay the same size as water pressure is uniform

topic: How does a hydraulic lift lift a car?
q1_text: What scientific principle makes a hydraulic lift able to lift a heavy car?
q1_a: Bernoulli's principle: fast-moving fluid creates lift under the car
q1_b: Pascal's law: pressure applied to a fluid is transmitted equally in all directions
q1_c: Archimedes' principle: the oil displaces the car's weight upward
q2_text: Why is understanding Pascal's law more useful than just knowing hydraulics work?
q2_a: Knowing hydraulics work is sufficient for designing all mechanical systems
q2_b: Pascal's law only applies to water, not to the oil used in hydraulics
q2_c: It lets engineers calculate piston sizes needed to lift any given load
q3_text: If the output piston area of a hydraulic lift were doubled, what would you predict?
q3_a: The lift force would be halved because more area reduces the pressure
q3_b: The fluid would flow backwards and the car would be lowered instead
q3_c: The lift force would double, allowing the system to lift twice the load

topic: How does an electric motor work?
q1_text: What causes an electric motor to rotate?
q1_a: A current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a force, causing rotation
q1_b: Electric charge builds up on the coil and repels the outer casing
q1_c: Heating of the wire by current causes it to expand and spin
q2_text: Why is understanding the motor mechanism more useful than knowing it spins?
q2_a: It helps engineers design motors with the correct power and efficiency
q2_b: Knowing the motor spins is sufficient for all electrical engineering work
q2_c: The motor mechanism only applies to DC motors, not AC motors
q3_text: If the magnetic field in a motor were made stronger, what would you predict?
q3_a: The motor would stop spinning because stronger fields oppose current flow
q3_b: The motor would produce more torque and rotate with greater force
q3_c: The motor coil would resist rotation due to greater electromagnetic induction

topic: How does a generator produce electricity?
q1_text: What is the basic mechanism by which a generator produces electricity?
q1_a: A generator stores static charge and releases it as a current when needed
q1_b: Chemical reactions inside the generator convert stored energy directly to current
q1_c: A coil rotating in a magnetic field induces an electric current by electromagnetic induction
q2_text: Why is understanding electromagnetic induction more useful than knowing generators make electricity?
q2_a: Knowing generators make electricity is sufficient for all power engineering
q2_b: Induction mechanisms only apply to alternators, not to simple DC generators
q2_c: It allows engineers to predict output voltage and design efficient power systems
q3_text: If a generator's coil spun twice as fast, what would you predict about the output?
q3_a: The output voltage would decrease because faster rotation weakens the field
q3_b: The output would stay constant because voltage depends only on coil size
q3_c: The output voltage and frequency would both increase

topic: Why does lightning happen?
q1_text: What causes the electrical discharge we see as lightning?
q1_a: Friction between raindrops and clouds produces heat that glows as lightning
q1_b: Oxygen in clouds reacts with nitrogen and releases energy as a bright flash
q1_c: Charge separation in clouds builds up until electrical discharge jumps to ground
q2_text: Why is understanding the charge-separation mechanism more useful than knowing lightning is dangerous?
q2_a: Knowing lightning is dangerous is sufficient for all safety applications
q2_b: The mechanism only explains cloud-to-ground lightning, not cloud-to-cloud
q2_c: It helps design lightning rods and predict storm behaviour accurately
q3_text: If a tall metal rod were placed on a building during a storm, what would you predict?
q3_a: The rod would attract more lightning and cause more damage to the building
q3_b: The rod would repel lightning by creating a magnetic field around the building
q3_c: Lightning would strike the rod and safely conduct charge to the ground

topic: How does a mobile phone transmit information?
q1_text: How does a mobile phone send information wirelessly?
q1_a: It sends electrical pulses through underground copper cables to towers
q1_b: It converts data into electromagnetic radio waves that travel to a cell tower
q1_c: It beams laser light signals directly to satellites in low orbit
q2_text: Why is understanding radio wave transmission more useful than knowing phones communicate?
q2_a: It helps engineers improve signal strength, bandwidth, and network coverage
q2_b: Knowing phones communicate wirelessly is sufficient for all telecom work
q2_c: Radio wave mechanisms only apply to older 2G networks, not 4G or 5G
q3_text: If you moved to an area with no cell towers nearby, what would you predict?
q3_a: The phone would automatically switch to satellite mode for full signal
q3_b: Signal strength would drop and calls and data would fail or disconnect
q3_c: Phone signals would become stronger as they spread out more in open space

topic: What is actually happening inside a chemical reaction?
q1_text: What actually happens at the molecular level during a chemical reaction?
q1_a: Atoms are destroyed and new atoms are created from energy in the reaction
q1_b: Bonds between atoms break and new bonds form, creating different substances
q1_c: Molecules are compressed until they merge into a new larger molecule
q2_text: Why is understanding bond-breaking and bond-forming more useful than memorising reaction products?
q2_a: It allows prediction of energy changes and products in new reactions
q2_b: Memorising products is sufficient since all reactions behave the same way
q2_c: Bond mechanisms only apply to organic chemistry, not inorganic reactions
q3_text: If a catalyst were added to a chemical reaction, what would you predict?
q3_a: The reaction would stop because catalysts block bond-breaking pathways
q3_b: New atoms would form because catalysts provide extra chemical energy
q3_c: The reaction would speed up as the catalyst lowers activation energy

topic: Why does fire need oxygen?
q1_text: Why is oxygen essential for fire to burn?
q1_a: Oxygen cools the fuel so it does not overheat and extinguish itself
q1_b: Oxygen carries the flame from one fuel molecule to the next by conduction
q1_c: Oxygen reacts with fuel in combustion, releasing heat and light energy
q2_text: Why is understanding combustion mechanism more useful than knowing fire needs oxygen?
q2_a: Knowing fire needs oxygen is enough to understand all fire safety situations
q2_b: It helps predict what conditions will start, sustain, or extinguish a fire
q2_c: Combustion mechanisms only apply to wood fires, not to gas or liquid fuels
q3_text: If all oxygen were removed from around a burning candle, what would you predict?
q3_a: The flame would go out immediately because combustion cannot continue
q3_b: The candle would burn more slowly but continue for several more minutes
q3_c: The flame would get smaller but stabilise once it adapts to lower oxygen

topic: Why do metals conduct electricity?
q1_text: What property of metals allows them to conduct electricity?
q1_a: Metals are dense, so charge squeezes through the material under pressure
q1_b: Metals have free electrons that move easily through the atomic lattice
q1_c: Metal atoms are positively charged and attract current from the source
q2_text: Why is knowing about free electrons more useful than just knowing metals conduct?
q2_a: Knowing metals conduct is sufficient to design all electrical circuits
q2_b: Free electron theory only explains conductivity in copper, not all metals
q2_c: It predicts how temperature and impurities affect conductivity in metals
q3_text: If a metal were heated to very high temperature, what would you predict about its resistance?
q3_a: Resistance would decrease because heat gives electrons more energy to move
q3_b: Resistance would increase because atomic vibrations disrupt electron flow
q3_c: Resistance would stay the same as temperature does not affect electrons

topic: How is steel different from iron?
q1_text: What makes steel stronger than pure iron?
q1_a: Steel contains carbon atoms that fill gaps in the iron lattice, blocking dislocations
q1_b: Steel is heated at higher temperatures, which permanently increases its density
q1_c: Steel has fewer iron atoms per unit area, making it lighter and more flexible
q2_text: Why does understanding the iron-carbon structure matter more than knowing steel is stronger?
q2_a: Knowing steel is stronger is sufficient for all construction and engineering
q2_b: The structural difference only matters for high-carbon steel, not mild steel
q2_c: It allows metallurgists to predict how changing carbon content alters properties
q3_text: If too much carbon were added to iron, what would you predict about the resulting material?
q3_a: The material would become even stronger and more ductile than normal steel
q3_b: The extra carbon would be expelled as carbon dioxide, returning it to iron
q3_c: The material would become very brittle and crack easily under stress

topic: Plastics: miracle material or environmental problem?
q1_text: What is the main reason plastics persist so long in the environment?
q1_a: Plastics contain toxins that kill the bacteria needed to decompose them
q1_b: Plastics are always coated with wax that prevents moisture from entering
q1_c: Most plastics are non-biodegradable polymers that microbes cannot break down
q2_text: Why is understanding the chemistry of plastic degradation important?
q2_a: Knowing plastic lasts long is sufficient for all environmental planning
q2_b: Degradation chemistry only matters for single-use plastics, not durable ones
q2_c: It guides development of biodegradable alternatives and recycling strategies
q3_text: If a biodegradable plastic were designed using natural polymers, what would you predict?
q3_a: Microbes could break it down naturally, reducing long-term environmental pollution
q3_b: It would last longer than regular plastic because natural polymers are stronger
q3_c: Microbes would still be unable to break it down because the shape is similar

topic: How do crops get nitrogen?
q1_text: How do most crops obtain the nitrogen they need to grow?
q1_a: Nitrogen is absorbed from soil as nitrates via roots, often aided by bacteria
q1_b: Crops absorb nitrogen gas directly from the air through their leaves
q1_c: Nitrogen enters plants through photosynthesis when sunlight splits nitrogen gas
q2_text: Why is understanding the nitrogen cycle mechanism more useful than knowing plants need nitrogen?
q2_a: It explains why crop rotation and fertilisers improve agricultural yields
q2_b: Knowing plants need nitrogen is enough to manage all farmland effectively
q2_c: Nitrogen mechanisms only matter for legumes, not for grains like wheat
q3_text: If nitrogen-fixing bacteria were removed from the soil, what would you predict?
q3_a: Soil nitrogen levels would drop and crops would suffer from nitrogen deficiency
q3_b: Plants would absorb more atmospheric nitrogen to compensate for the loss
q3_c: Soil nitrogen levels would stay constant as rainfall deposits enough nitrogen

topic: Why are some animals disappearing?
q1_text: What is the leading cause of animal species becoming endangered today?
q1_a: Genetic mutations are making animals less able to survive natural conditions
q1_b: Habitat destruction reduces living space and food sources for wildlife
q1_c: Competition between species has recently increased due to climate cooling
q2_text: Why is understanding extinction mechanisms more useful than listing endangered species?
q2_a: Species lists are sufficient to plan all conservation efforts worldwide
q2_b: Mechanisms help conservationists target the root causes and reverse decline
q2_c: Extinction mechanisms only apply to large mammals, not insects or plants
q3_text: If a keystone species disappeared from an ecosystem, what would you predict?
q3_a: Multiple species that depended on it would decline, disrupting the ecosystem
q3_b: Other species would quickly evolve to fill the role and restore balance
q3_c: Only the immediate prey species would be affected; predators would adapt

topic: How does a food chain work?
q1_text: What does a food chain show about energy in an ecosystem?
q1_a: A food chain shows the physical paths animals travel when searching for food
q1_b: A food chain records the order in which animals appeared during evolution
q1_c: A food chain shows how energy and nutrients are transferred from producers to consumers
q2_text: Why is understanding energy transfer in a food chain useful?
q2_a: Knowing which animals eat which others is sufficient for ecology studies
q2_b: Energy transfer only matters in marine food chains, not terrestrial ones
q2_c: It helps predict population sizes and the impact of removing one species
q3_text: If all herbivores in a food chain disappeared, what would you predict?
q3_a: Carnivores would switch directly to eating plants and survive without issue
q3_b: Carnivores would lose their food source and decline, while plants overgrew
q3_c: Plant populations would decrease because herbivores provide essential nutrients

topic: What happens when an ecosystem loses one species?
q1_text: What is a trophic cascade in an ecosystem?
q1_a: When a new species enters and immediately occupies the top of the food chain
q1_b: When removing one species causes a chain reaction affecting many other species
q1_c: When flooding events rearrange species populations across large areas
q2_text: Why is understanding species interdependence more useful than knowing a species is gone?
q2_a: Recording that a species is extinct is sufficient for ecological management
q2_b: Interdependence only matters in tropical rainforests, not temperate ecosystems
q2_c: It allows scientists to predict and prevent collapse of entire ecosystems
q3_text: If wolves were reintroduced to an ecosystem where they had been absent, what would you predict?
q3_a: Deer populations would decline, allowing vegetation to recover along riverbanks
q3_b: Only deer populations would be affected; all other species would be unchanged
q3_c: Wolves would compete with herbivores directly and reduce plant diversity

topic: How does rainwater become groundwater?
q1_text: How does rainwater become groundwater stored underground?
q1_a: Rainwater is absorbed by tree roots and stored in underground hollow trunks
q1_b: Rainwater infiltrates through permeable soil and rock layers into aquifers
q1_c: Rainwater evaporates and then condenses in underground caves as groundwater
q2_text: Why is understanding the infiltration mechanism more useful than knowing groundwater exists?
q2_a: Knowing groundwater exists is sufficient for all water management decisions
q2_b: It helps predict aquifer recharge rates and sustainable water extraction limits
q2_c: Infiltration only matters in sandy soils, not in clay-rich or rocky terrain
q3_text: If forests covering a hillside were cleared, what would you predict about groundwater recharge?
q3_a: More rain would reach the soil directly, increasing groundwater recharge
q3_b: Groundwater levels would stay the same because rainfall amount is unchanged
q3_c: Surface runoff would increase and infiltration would decrease, reducing recharge

topic: Why do cyclones rotate?
q1_text: What causes a cyclone to rotate rather than move straight inward?
q1_a: Warm ocean water heats air unevenly, pushing it into a spinning column
q1_b: High-altitude jet streams catch rising air and force it into a circular path
q1_c: The Coriolis effect from Earth's rotation deflects winds, causing circular motion
q2_text: Why is understanding the Coriolis effect and pressure gradient more useful than knowing cyclones spin?
q2_a: Knowing cyclones spin is enough to issue storm warnings to coastal areas
q2_b: It enables accurate prediction of cyclone paths, intensity, and timing
q2_c: Rotation mechanisms only explain cyclones, not anticyclones or tornadoes
q3_text: If a cyclone crossed the equator, what would you predict about its rotation?
q3_a: It would accelerate because the equator has the strongest Coriolis effect
q3_b: It would weaken and dissipate because the Coriolis effect is zero at the equator
q3_c: It would maintain its original rotation direction as momentum is conserved

topic: How do satellites stay in orbit?
q1_text: Why doesn't a satellite fall to Earth even though gravity pulls on it?
q1_a: The satellite reaches an altitude where gravity is too weak to pull it down
q1_b: Solar panels on the satellite produce thrust that counteracts gravitational pull
q1_c: The satellite moves so fast sideways that it keeps falling around Earth's curve
q2_text: Why is understanding orbital mechanics more useful than just knowing satellites stay up?
q2_a: Knowing satellites stay in orbit is sufficient for all space mission planning
q2_b: Orbital mechanics only apply to large satellites, not to small cubesats
q2_c: It allows engineers to calculate correct launch speeds and orbital altitudes
q3_text: If a satellite were slowed down significantly by atmospheric drag, what would you predict?
q3_a: The satellite would move to a higher orbit because lower speed saves fuel
q3_b: The satellite's orbit would decay and it would eventually fall back to Earth
q3_c: The satellite would orbit in a wider ellipse but remain at the same altitude

topic: Why doesn't the Moon fall onto Earth?
q1_text: Why doesn't the Moon crash into Earth despite gravity pulling them together?
q1_a: The Moon's orbital speed creates a balance between gravity and inertia
q1_b: The Moon is pushed away from Earth by the solar wind balancing gravity
q1_c: Earth's gravity is too weak at that distance to pull the Moon
q2_text: Why is understanding orbital balance more useful than knowing the Moon stays in the sky?
q2_a: Knowing the Moon stays up is sufficient for all astronomy and tidal studies
q2_b: Orbital balance only applies to natural moons, not to artificial satellites
q2_c: It explains how any orbiting body can be stable and predicts orbital changes
q3_text: If the Moon's orbital speed suddenly decreased, what would you predict?
q3_a: The Moon would move to a higher orbit due to reduced centripetal acceleration
q3_b: The Moon would spiral inward toward Earth as gravity overcame its inertia
q3_c: Earth's gravity would weaken proportionally to maintain the Moon's orbit

topic: Could we build a city underwater?
q1_text: What is the greatest engineering challenge for building a city underwater?
q1_a: Finding enough sand on the ocean floor to build foundations
q1_b: Generating enough heat to keep inhabitants warm in deep water
q1_c: Withstanding enormous water pressure that increases with depth
q2_text: Why is understanding fluid pressure mechanisms important for underwater city design?
q2_a: Knowing water is heavy is sufficient to plan all underwater construction
q2_b: It determines the structural materials and wall thickness needed for safety
q2_c: Pressure mechanisms only matter for military submarines, not civilian structures
q3_text: If an underwater habitat were built at twice the depth, what would you predict about its walls?
q3_a: Much thicker and stronger walls would be needed to withstand doubled pressure
q3_b: Thinner walls would be needed as deeper water provides extra structural support
q3_c: Wall thickness would remain the same if the same waterproof material is used

topic: Ultimate Challenge: Design a future sustainable city
q1_text: What is the central goal when designing a sustainable city?
q1_a: Meeting all human needs while minimising resource use and environmental impact
q1_b: Building as many tall buildings as possible to house the largest population
q1_c: Using the most advanced technology regardless of energy or material cost
q2_text: Why is a systems-thinking approach more useful than solving one problem at a time?
q2_a: Sustainable city systems are interconnected; fixing one part affects all others
q2_b: Solving individual problems one by one is the most efficient design strategy
q2_c: Systems thinking only applies to large cities with over one million residents
q3_text: If a sustainable city removed all cars and relied only on cycling and walking, what would you predict?
q3_a: Air quality and public health would improve and carbon emissions would drop
q3_b: Air pollution would increase because more people outdoors release more CO2
q3_c: Energy demand would increase because more lighting would be needed on paths

topic: What is matter really made of?
q1_text: Which best describes what matter is made of at its most fundamental level?
q1_a: Matter is made of continuous, unbroken fluid that fills all space
q1_b: Matter is made of invisible waves that have no mass
q1_c: Matter is made of tiny particles called atoms and molecules
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism more useful than just memorising the result?
q2_a: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_b: Mechanisms are shorter to write and easier to remember in exams
q2_c: Mechanisms are always visible so they are easier to verify directly
q3_text: If the number of particles in a fixed space were doubled, what would you predict?
q3_a: The particles would slow down and stop moving entirely
q3_b: The density of matter would increase and collisions between particles would rise
q3_c: The particles would merge into one large continuous substance

topic: Why do particles move even when you can't see them?
q1_text: What is the main reason particles in matter are always in motion?
q1_a: Particles possess kinetic energy and move continuously at all temperatures above absolute zero
q1_b: Particles are pushed by gravity which keeps them vibrating constantly
q1_c: Particles move only when an external force such as wind acts on them
q2_text: Why is knowing the mechanism of particle motion more useful than just knowing they move?
q2_a: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_b: It saves time because you only need to learn one fact about motion
q2_c: Mechanisms are easier to draw in diagrams than descriptions of motion
q3_text: If temperature were lowered toward absolute zero, what would happen to particle motion?
q3_a: Particle motion would increase because cold particles vibrate more rapidly
q3_b: Particle motion would stay constant because temperature does not affect speed
q3_c: Particle motion would approach zero as thermal energy is removed from the system

topic: How does diffusion work?
q1_text: What correctly describes diffusion?
q1_a: Diffusion is the movement of water molecules only through a semipermeable membrane
q1_b: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from high concentration toward low concentration
q1_c: Diffusion is the process by which particles clump together under gravitational attraction
q2_text: Why is understanding the mechanism of diffusion more useful than memorising the definition?
q2_a: Definitions are hard to remember, while mechanisms can be guessed from context
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: Mechanisms are tested less frequently in school examinations than definitions
q3_text: If temperature were increased, what would you predict about the rate of diffusion?
q3_a: Diffusion would slow down because higher temperature makes particles too energetic to spread
q3_b: Diffusion would stop because particles become too heavy at high temperatures
q3_c: Diffusion would speed up because higher temperature increases particle kinetic energy

topic: Why does temperature change particle motion?
q1_text: What is the relationship between temperature and the kinetic energy of particles?
q1_a: Temperature measures the total potential energy stored in chemical bonds between particles
q1_b: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance
q1_c: Temperature measures the number of particles present in a given volume of substance
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism linking temperature and particle motion important?
q2_a: It allows students to skip calculations and focus on written descriptions only
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: It is required only for physics and not for chemistry or biology topics
q3_text: If a gas were cooled significantly, what change in particle motion would you predict?
q3_a: The particles would gain energy and collide more forcefully with container walls
q3_b: The particles would slow down and may eventually condense into a liquid or solid
q3_c: The particles would reorganise into a new element with different chemical properties

topic: Atoms: the tiny building blocks of everything
q1_text: Which statement best describes an atom?
q1_a: An atom is a cluster of molecules held together by surface tension forces
q1_b: An atom is the smallest unit of an element retaining that element's chemical properties
q1_c: An atom is a unit of energy that cannot be divided by any known process
q2_text: Why is understanding how atoms behave more useful than just memorising their definition?
q2_a: Definitions are optional knowledge, while behaviour is tested in every examination
q2_b: Atomic behaviour is simpler to learn because it involves only three rules
q2_c: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q3_text: If the number of protons in an atom were changed, what would you predict?
q3_a: The mass of the atom would stay identical because protons have negligible mass
q3_b: The atom would become a different element with different chemical properties
q3_c: The atom's electron shells would collapse because electrons depend on neutrons

topic: How was the atom discovered?
q1_text: Which experiment provided the first evidence that the atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus?
q1_a: Dalton's law experiment, where gases combined in fixed volume ratios at constant pressure
q1_b: Thomson's cathode ray experiment, which showed that electrons orbit the nucleus in shells
q1_c: Rutherford's gold foil experiment, where alpha particles were deflected at large angles
q2_text: Why is knowing the mechanism of the gold foil experiment more valuable than memorising its result?
q2_a: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_b: Results change every year but mechanisms stay constant and are never re-examined
q2_c: The mechanism involves maths which is more reliable than descriptive results
q3_text: If all alpha particles had passed straight through the gold foil without deflection, what would that predict?
q3_a: The nucleus would be confirmed to be large and spread throughout the atom
q3_b: The experiment would show that electrons repel alpha particles near the surface
q3_c: The atom would likely have no dense nucleus, contradicting the nuclear model

topic: Why are some atoms radioactive?
q1_text: What causes an atom to be radioactive?
q1_a: An unstable nucleus spontaneously emits radiation to achieve a more stable nuclear configuration
q1_b: An atom becomes radioactive when it gains extra electrons from a nearby charged object
q1_c: Radioactivity occurs when atoms absorb too much sunlight and re-emit it as particles
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism of radioactive decay more useful than just knowing it emits radiation?
q2_a: Knowing radiation exists is sufficient for safety; mechanisms are only for scientists
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: The mechanism helps calculate tax on nuclear materials in industrial settings
q3_text: If a radioactive isotope lost neutrons until its nucleus became stable, what would you predict?
q3_a: The atom would continue emitting stronger and stronger radiation indefinitely
q3_b: The rate of radioactive emission would decrease and eventually the atom would become stable
q3_c: The atom would split into two equal halves and both halves would remain radioactive

topic: What makes an element different from another?
q1_text: What property uniquely identifies and distinguishes one element from all others?
q1_a: The colour and texture of the element in its solid form at room temperature
q1_b: The total mass of the element including all isotopes averaged across the periodic table
q1_c: The number of protons in the nucleus, the atomic number, uniquely defines each element
q2_text: Why is understanding the mechanism that makes elements different more valuable than listing their properties?
q2_a: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_b: Properties change with temperature, making them less reliable than any mechanism
q2_c: Listing properties is required for industrial applications while mechanisms are theoretical
q3_text: If two atoms had the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, what would you predict?
q3_a: They would be completely different elements with entirely different chemical behaviours
q3_b: They would be oppositely charged ions that attract each other strongly in solution
q3_c: They would be isotopes of the same element with slightly different masses but similar chemistry

topic: How do chemical bonds hold matter together?
q1_text: What is the correct description of how ionic bonds form?
q1_a: Ionic bonds form when two atoms share electrons equally in overlapping outer orbitals
q1_b: Ionic bonds form when atoms merge their nuclei together under high temperature and pressure
q1_c: Ionic bonds form when one atom transfers electrons to another, creating attracting oppositely charged ions
q2_text: Why is knowing the mechanism of chemical bonding more useful than memorising bond definitions?
q2_a: Bond definitions are too long to memorise, so mechanisms replace them in advanced study
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: Mechanisms are shorter and therefore easier to write in limited examination time
q3_text: If an atom with one outer electron bonded with an atom that needed one electron, what would form?
q3_a: An ionic compound where the electron transfers, forming a positive and negative ion pair
q3_b: A covalent compound where both atoms share their electrons equally across all shells
q3_c: A metallic lattice because single-electron atoms always form metallic structures

topic: Why does mass stay conserved in a reaction?
q1_text: What does the law of conservation of mass state about a chemical reaction?
q1_a: Mass increases in every reaction because energy is converted into additional matter
q1_b: Mass is conserved only in physical changes but always changes in chemical reactions
q1_c: Total reactant mass equals total product mass; atoms are neither created nor destroyed
q2_text: Why is understanding the atomic mechanism of mass conservation more useful than just stating the law?
q2_a: The law is outdated, so the mechanism provides a more modern and accurate description
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: Memorising the law is sufficient for all practical laboratory and industrial purposes
q3_text: If a metal burned completely in air and the ash seemed lighter, what prediction explains this correctly?
q3_a: Some atoms were destroyed in the intense heat of the combustion reaction
q3_b: Some product gases escaped into the air; total mass including gases is still conserved
q3_c: The metal released protons that escaped into the atmosphere, reducing its mass

topic: How does your body obtain energy from food?
q1_text: What process does the body use to release energy from glucose for cellular use?
q1_a: Cellular respiration breaks down glucose using oxygen, releasing energy stored as ATP
q1_b: Digestion converts glucose directly into electricity that powers muscle contractions
q1_c: Photosynthesis in red blood cells converts glucose into usable heat energy
q2_text: Why is knowing the mechanism of energy release more useful than just knowing food gives energy?
q2_a: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_b: Food labels describe energy content, making mechanism knowledge unnecessary in practice
q2_c: Mechanisms are only relevant for athletes and not for average healthy individuals
q3_text: If oxygen supply to cells were cut off, what would you predict about energy production?
q3_a: Energy production would increase because cells switch to a more efficient pathway
q3_b: Energy production would remain normal because mitochondria store enough reserve oxygen
q3_c: Aerobic respiration would stop and cells would rely on less efficient anaerobic respiration

topic: The architecture of a cell
q1_text: Which structure controls all activities of the cell and contains its genetic material?
q1_a: The nucleus, which houses DNA and directs all cellular processes and protein synthesis
